summary: Describes TLS cipher suites that combine the AES-CCM encryption mode with elliptic curve cryptography. AES-CCM can be implemented compactly, which makes it a good fit for constrained devices and low-bandwidth networks.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a recipe for scrambling messages that is small enough for tiny gadgets to cook. It keeps messages secret and shows that they were not changed.

subtitle: Compact encryption recipes for small devices and limited bandwidth networks.

tldr.problem: Devices with limited memory and power, and networks with limited bandwidth, need secure TLS cipher suites that are more compact than existing options.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7251 defines TLS cipher suites that combine AES-CCM (Counter with CBC-MAC mode) encryption with Elliptic Curve Cryptography for key exchange, using only the AES block cipher operation and no additional primitives.
tldr.outcome: These cipher suites enable TLS on resource-constrained devices (like embedded servers and IoT endpoints) while maintaining strong security. They work with TLS 1.2 and DTLS for unreliable networks.

today: RFC 7251 is an Informational RFC published in June 2014. These cipher suites are widely supported in modern TLS libraries and are particularly important for embedded systems, IoT devices, and wireless networks like 802.15.4 and mobile networks that require both strong security and minimal overhead. They remain relevant for any deployment where resource constraints are a concern.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 7251 defines a set of TLS cipher suites for systems with limited resources, such as embedded servers and devices on low-bandwidth networks. These suites use the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Counter with CBC-MAC Mode (AES-CCM), which provides both confidentiality and data-origin authentication. Unlike some encryption modes that require separate operations, AES-CCM uses only the AES block cipher as its single primitive, making it compact enough to fit in memory-constrained environments. The cipher suites also use Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) for key exchange, which requires shorter cryptographic keys than traditional methods while maintaining security. These suites work with TLS 1.2 and can also be used with DTLS (Datagram TLS) for unreliable networks.
sections.plainLanguage: This recipe uses a method that is small to implement but still very safe. It scrambles messages in a way that is both safe and uses very little memory.

sections.title: The Cipher Suites
sections.content:
Four TLS cipher suites are defined, each using ECDHE (Ephemeral Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman) for key agreement and ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) for authentication:

  • TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM uses 128-bit AES with a 16-octet (128-bit) authentication tag,
  • TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_CCM uses 256-bit AES with a 16-octet authentication tag,
  • TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 uses 128-bit AES with an 8-octet (64-bit) authentication tag (suitable for bandwidth-constrained networks),
  • TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_CCM_8 uses 256-bit AES with an 8-octet authentication tag.

The shorter authentication tags (with _8 in the name) reduce the overhead for networks where bandwidth is extremely limited, such as IoT networks. All of these cipher suites require TLS 1.2 or later and MUST NOT be negotiated in older versions of TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four ways to scramble with this recipe. Two use bigger locks (256-bit) and two use smaller locks (128-bit). Two also use smaller seals (8-bit tags) for when you do not have much room to write.

sections.title: Key Exchange and Cryptographic Algorithms
sections.content: The cipher suites use ECDHE for key establishment, meaning the client and server jointly create a session key using ephemeral (temporary) elliptic curve keys. This ensures that even if a long-term key is later compromised, past sessions remain secure (a property called perfect forward secrecy). The server's certificate MUST contain an ECDSA-capable public key and be signed with ECDSA. The uncompressed point format for elliptic curve points MUST be supported; other formats MAY be used. Implementations SHOULD use elliptic curves with a cofactor of one, which simplifies their use. The cipher suites use the TLS 1.2 Pseudorandom Function, which relies on HMAC with SHA-256 to derive the final encryption keys from the shared secret.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server each pick a secret number, mix them together in a special way, and end up with the same secret only they know. This way, if someone steals the server's secret later, they still cannot figure out what this conversation was.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: AES-CCM security requires that the counter value never be reused with the same key. The nonce (initialization value) construction in the RFC is designed to prevent counter reuse in both TLS and DTLS environments. In DTLS, the 64-bit sequence number field is built from a 16-bit epoch and a 48-bit sequence number, allowing an internal 32-bit counter that is convenient for CCM. Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) require special handling when used with these cipher suites because the nonce salt is derived from the TLS master secret. Additionally, the CCM decrypt operation cannot use the DecryptUpdate function in typical cryptographic interfaces because the plaintext must not be returned until the authentication check is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The scrambling machine must never use the same counter twice with the same key, or the magic breaks. Special hardware vaults need extra care when using these recipes.

sections.title: Recommended Curves and Algorithms
sections.content: The RFC does not mandate any specific elliptic curves or hash functions, allowing flexibility. However, recommended choices for interoperability and security are provided. For 128-bit AES suites, implementations SHOULD support the secp256r1 curve and SHA-256 hash function. For 256-bit AES suites, implementations SHOULD support the secp384r1 curve and SHA-384 hash function, and MAY also support the secp521r1 curve with SHA-512. Other curves, such as the Brainpool curves, are acceptable if they meet the same security level requirements. The RFC motivates these cipher suites through the needs of constrained devices and networks, including Zigbee Smart Energy deployments, where compact implementations are essential.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipe says which locks and keys work best together. The smallest locks pair with smaller numbers, and the biggest locks pair with bigger numbers. Different kitchens can use different ingredient brands as long as they are the right strength.
